issues.legal_issue: An interlocutory mandatory injunction may be granted where the applicant has a strong case for trial, the injunction is needed to prevent serious irreparable injury, and the balance of convenience favours the applicant.
material_facts: The applicant sought an interim order requiring a purchaser who had entered the disputed property to leave it while the suit was pending.
The trial court granted the interim order, but the High Court set it aside; the applicant appealed.
issues.conclusion: Courts have power to grant interlocutory mandatory injunctions in special circumstances. The applicant must generally show a case for trial stronger than the ordinary prima facie case, the necessity of preventing irreparable or serious injury, and that the balance of convenience favours the applicant; the ultimate decision remains within the court’s equitable discretion.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles in Shepherd Homes Ltd. v. Sandham, Evans Marshall & Co. Ltd. v. Bertola SA, and Films Rover International Ltd. v. Cannon Film Sales Ltd. It also relied on Rasul Karim v. Pirubhai Amirbhai, Champsey Bhimji & Co. v. The Jamna Flour Mills Co. Ltd., M. Kandaswami Chetty v. P. Subramania Chetty, Israil v. Shamser Rahman, and Nandan Pictures Ltd. v. Art Pictures Ltd. The guidelines are not exhaustive or absolute; the remedy is equitable and must be exercised judicially in the circumstances of each case.

rule.if: interlocutory_mandatory_injunction_sought and strong_case_for_trial and serious_irreparable_injury_needs_prevention and balance_of_convenience_favors_applicant

predicates.interlocutory_mandatory_injunction_sough: A party to a pending proceeding asks the court for an interim order requiring another party to do an act or undo an act.
predicates.strong_case_for_trial: The applicant’s case for obtaining the claimed relief at trial is stronger than the ordinary prima facie case required for a prohibitory injunction.
predicates.serious_irreparable_injury_needs_prevent: The requested order is necessary to prevent serious injury that ordinarily cannot be compensated with money.
predicates.balance_of_convenience_favors_applicant: The comparative inconvenience or harm from withholding the order is greater than that from granting it.

issues.definition: When an applicant seeks an interim mandatory order, has a strong case for trial, needs the order to prevent serious irreparable injury, and would suffer the greater comparative inconvenience if it were withheld, the court may grant the order in its equitable discretion.

issues.legal_issue: A dwelling house remains property of an undivided family for the restriction on a transferee’s joint possession when the family holds it as tenants in common but the property has not been divided by metes and bounds.
material_facts: The applicant and his brother held equal undivided shares in the house as tenants in common.
The evidence showed no partition of the house by metes and bounds.
The brother’s heirs transferred their undivided share to a purchaser who was not a member of the family.
The applicant’s family and his brother’s family had occupied different portions, but this did not establish a partition of the property by metes and bounds.
issues.conclusion: At the interlocutory stage, there was a prima facie case that the house belonged to an undivided family. Severance of status and ownership as tenants in common did not take the house outside the restriction where it remained undivided by metes and bounds; the stranger transferee was not entitled to joint possession.
issues.legal_principle: The second paragraph of section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act applies where a share in a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family is transferred to someone outside the family. The terms “undivided family” and “dwelling house” have the same meaning in section 44 and section 4 of the Partition Act, whose provisions are complementary. The family need not be a Hindu joint family, and a division in status or separate occupation of portions does not by itself amount to division of the house by metes and bounds. The Court relied on Sultan Begam v. Debi Prasad, Khirode Chandra Ghoshal v. Saroda Prasad Mitra, Nil Kamal Bhattacharjya v. Kamakshya Charan Bhattacharjya, Sivaramayya v. Venkata Subbamma, Bhim Singh v. Ratnakar, and Udayanath Sahu v. Ratnakar Bej.

rule.if: co_ownership_dwelling_house_dispute and dwelling_house_owned_by_family and property_not_divided_by_metes_and_bounds and share_transferred_to_family_outsider

predicates.co_ownership_dwelling_house_dispute: The proceeding concerns co-owners’ rights in a house used as a dwelling.
predicates.dwelling_house_owned_by_family: The house is owned by members of a family as co-owners and is treated as belonging to that family.
predicates.property_not_divided_by_metes_and_bounds: The house has not been physically partitioned into separate ownership portions, even if family members have separated in status or use different portions.
predicates.share_transferred_to_family_outsider: A co-owner transfers a share in the house to a person who is not a member of the family.

issues.definition: When family members co-own a dwelling house that has not been divided into separate portions and a share is transferred to an outsider, the outsider is not entitled to joint possession.

issues.legal_issue: A court may order an outsider who has taken possession of an undivided family dwelling house to yield possession by interim mandatory injunction where the applicant has a strong prima facie claim, faces irreparable injury, and the balance of convenience favours restoration, particularly when the outsider knowingly and clandestinely sought to forestall legal relief.
material_facts: The purchaser’s agreement showed awareness that the sellers’ share was subject to the other family member’s rights and that litigation was contemplated.
The sale and entry into possession occurred hurriedly and secretly, before the applicant could obtain effective relief.
The applicant filed suit shortly after the sale and obtained an interim order, but the purchaser had already entered the premises.
The applicant had a prima facie case that the house remained undivided and that the purchaser, as an outsider, could not claim joint possession.
The Court found that withholding the injunction would cause irreparable injury and that the balance of convenience favoured the applicant.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court’s decision, and restored the trial court’s interim mandatory injunction requiring the purchaser to cease possession or enjoyment of the disputed property. The Court stated that its factual observations were not binding at the final trial and that the vendors could ask the trial court for permission to return to the portion they had previously occupied.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the interlocutory mandatory injunction guidelines and, in a proceeding concerning an undivided family dwelling house, took account of the restriction on an outsider transferee’s joint possession under section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Court relied on the principle that the transferee’s entry into possession does not defeat the family member’s claim where the transferee is legally barred from joint possession; it approved the statement of law in Bhim Singh v. Ratnakar and referred to Udayanath Sahu v. Ratnakar Bej. A party who knowingly acts to forestall the other party’s recourse to court cannot rely on that conduct to defeat the claim for interim relief.

rule.if: co_ownership_dwelling_house_suit and strong_prima_facie_claim_to_exclude_outsider and outsider_already_in_possession and serious_irreparable_injury_from_withholding_relief and balance_of_convenience_favors_applicant and outsider_knowingly_rushed_to_forestal_relief

predicates.co_ownership_dwelling_house_suit: A party seeks interim relief in a dispute over an outsider’s possession of a co-owned family dwelling house.
predicates.strong_prima_facie_claim_to_exclude_outs: The applicant has a strong preliminary case that the house remains undivided family property and that the outsider is not entitled to joint possession.
predicates.outsider_already_in_possession: The outsider has entered and taken possession of some or all of the disputed property before the court decides the interim application.
predicates.serious_irreparable_injury_from_withhold: Leaving the outsider in possession pending trial would cause the applicant serious harm that cannot ordinarily be compensated with money.
predicates.balance_of_convenience_favors_applicant: The harm or inconvenience from withholding the order is greater than that from requiring the outsider to yield possession.
predicates.outsider_knowingly_rushed_to_forestal_re: The outsider knew of the applicant’s asserted rights and hurried or concealed the transaction or entry in a manner intended to forestall the applicant’s recourse to court.

issues.definition: In a co-ownership dwelling-house suit, an outsider who has taken possession despite a strong preliminary claim to exclude the outsider must yield possession by interim order when withholding relief would cause irreparable injury, the balance favours the applicant, and the outsider knowingly rushed to forestall relief.
